# Brownsville seawater desalination: data sheet

Numbers are from the Lower Rio Grande Valley Brownsville Seawater Desalination Demonstration Project Feasibility Study (Dannenbaum Engineering and URS for the Brownsville Public Utilities Board, November 2004) (2004 PDF p.1). Citations are PDF page numbers of that study. The drawing is a PlantAgent sketch of the Section 4 flowsheet, not a copy of Figure 4-5 (2004 PDF p.182). Anything the study does not state is marked (ILLUSTRATIVE).

## Capacity

The concept is an initial 25 MGD finished-water plant that can be expanded to 100 MGD in 25 MGD increments (2004 PDF p.384). Five of six seawater RO trains produce the initial 25 MGD. The sixth train is the spare (2004 PDF p.195). Each seawater train is designed for 5 MGD of permeate (2004 PDF p.195).

## Source water

The intake is in side channels of the Brownsville Ship Channel (2004 PDF p.27). Ship-channel TDS in the reviewed record runs from about 11,700 ppm to about 49,000 ppm. The average near 36,100 ppm is why the study set aside the extreme single points, and the design range kept after that review is still 11,700 to 49,000 mg/L (2004 PDF p.112 and p.189). TSS is about 36 mg/L and has been as high as 153 mg/L (2004 PDF p.112). Temperature is typically 60 F to 95 F, annual average 75 F (2004 PDF p.192).

A full ion table comparable to a membrane projection is not printed in the sections cited here. ILLUSTRATIVE: do not fill missing ions from a standard seawater recipe and call it Brownsville data.

## Process

Intake screens are a copper-nickel alloy, sized to limit impingement and entrainment (2004 PDF p.186). Ballasted flocculation: three trains in parallel, each hydraulically rated for 21 MGD. Two trains carry the full finished-water capacity and the third is spare (2004 PDF p.186).

Steam from a co-located power plant preheats the RO feed. The study's rule of thumb is that high-pressure pump discharge pressure falls about 1 percent per degree Fahrenheit of feed heating. Heating the average 75 F water to 90 F is described as about a 15 percent pressure reduction (2004 PDF p.192). The heater is a 36 inch in-line steam heater on each feed stream (2004 PDF p.192).

Sulfuric acid may be used to hold about pH 6.5. If the seawater is already acidified ahead of ballasted flocculation, a further 20 mg/L of concentrated sulfuric acid is the study's figure to move pH from 7.0 to 6.0. Antiscalant is provided for even if piloting does not confirm the dose. The dose itself is not given (2004 PDF p.193). ILLUSTRATIVE: an antiscalant concentration in mg/L is not in the study.

Cartridge filters are the last barrier for solids larger than 5 microns (2004 PDF p.193).

Seawater RO: six parallel trains, 5 MGD permeate each, two stages, six-element pressure vessels, reject staging used to push overall recovery to about 60 percent. Brine is about 3.33 MGD per train, 16.67 MGD for the 25 MGD plant at that recovery (2004 PDF p.195). About 44 percent of the combined permeate goes to the partial second pass (2004 PDF p.195). First-pass TDS is described as falling from about 36,000 ppm to about 380 ppm (2004 PDF p.196).

Energy recovery selected in the screening is a Pelton wheel, one turbine per seawater train. The positive-displacement work exchanger was the other alternative and was not the preferred selection (2004 PDF p.145). Without energy recovery the study says each seawater high-pressure pump would be about 4,000 HP (2004 PDF p.143).

The conceptual-design pump for each seawater train is approximately 1,100 psig with a 2,900 HP variable-speed motor (2004 PDF p.197).
The mechanically coupled Pelton turbine contributes shaft work and is described as reducing electrical demand by about
33 percent (2004 PDF p.197). A motor check must therefore compare the motor with pump shaft demand net of the turbine,
not with the gross pump duty before recovered shaft work.

Second pass: two brackish trains, one of them spare. Each is rated for about 11.1 MGD of feed at the required pressure, with a 300 HP variable-speed drive. Recovery is about 90 percent. Concentrate is recycled ahead of the seawater trains so the composite recovery stays about 60 percent (2004 PDF p.195 and p.196).

Stabilization is intended to add about 40 mg/L of calcium. Both pebble lime and calcite filters were screened (2004 PDF p.144 and p.109). The study does not pick a finished-water boron limit in the pages used here.

Of the primary-treatment product, about 1.84 MGD (1,280 gpm) is identified as cooling-tower makeup for the co-located power plant, and about 0.16 MGD (110 gpm) as demineralized water (2004 PDF p.197).

Brine from the initial plant is 16.67 MGD at 60 percent recovery, as above. The diffuser appendix repeats the 25 MGD initial capacity, the 100 MGD build-out and the 60 percent recovery (2004 PDF p.384).

Power cost used for the heater example is 0.035 dollars per kWh (2004 PDF p.192). The comment responses in the front of the PDF say that tariff was already considered low and that the current municipal rate was higher; they do not replace it with a new number in the section cited (2004 PDF p.10).

## Not in the study

ILLUSTRATIVE if a model needs them: membrane area and flux (gfd is not stated in the sections above), element manufacturer, vessel count, intake-pump head, and a full ion recipe. The 2004 text says pilot testing would still be required for the acid dose and the antiscalant (2004 PDF p.193).

## Request

Can this 25 MGD concept hold about 60 percent overall recovery and the finished-water duty on the cold, salty corner of the ship-channel record (about 60 F and 49,000 mg/L TDS) with one seawater train out of service? What limits it first, and what is the cheapest way to stay at 25 MGD? Those corners are the study's own figures (2004 PDF p.112, p.192 and p.195).

submit.headline: No — cold salty corner falls short
submit.summary: At 60 °F and 49,000 mg/L, the logged run “baseline-cold-salty-1train” reaches only 47.2% recovery and 0.539 g/L permeate salt at the documented 75.84 bar pressure cap, against the study targets of about 60% recovery and 0.5 g/L in the model. No tested operating option using the existing documented pressure, pump motor or membrane limits passes; the cheapest credible route is new higher-pressure pumping and membrane-pressure equipment, vendor-quoted and re-solved before acceptance, so this conclusion is provisional on the missing membrane projection data noted below.

highlights.text: Limits first: at 60 °F and 49,000 mg/L the second stage reaches only 0.1387 recovery against its 0.333 design check and overall recovery is 0.472 against about 0.60 (runs baseline-cold-salty-1train, ro_capacity), at the 75.84 bar pressure cap.

Already at its documented about 1,100 psig discharge cap (75.84 bar, 2004 PDF p.197); a diagnostic 95 bar run reaches 60.6% recovery but is not permitted on this pump or the existing vessels and still gives 0.529 g/L salt (run pressure-scan-95bar).

Documented steam heating (60–95 °F channel range, P&ID E-101) does not rescue the corner in the simulator — 90 °F gives 0.442 recovery (run heat-90F-per-train) — and the heater is note-only in the model, so do not rely on it without a vendor projection.
Pretreatment is two duty plus one spare 21 MGD trains (P&ID F-101); it is not the first limit found in the cold-corner runs.

Second pass is one duty plus one spare 11.1 MGD-feed train at about 90% recovery (P&ID RO-301), but it is a documented note only in this model, so finished-water quality after the partial second pass is unproven here.

Brine diffuser is documented for 16.67 MGD at 60% recovery for the 25 MGD plant (P&ID D-601); at the simulated 47.2% recovery the brine flow would be larger, which needs checking before any low-recovery workaround is accepted.

proposals.title: Add a higher-pressure feed pump train — do not uprate the existing pump
proposals.why: The existing pump is already at its documented about 1,100 psig (75.84 bar) cap while recovery is only 47.2%; a diagnostic run at 95 bar is the first point that reaches about 60% recovery, so new, properly rated pumping is required rather than a setpoint increase (runs baseline-cold-salty-1train and pressure-scan-95bar).

proposals.title: Add a higher-pressure membrane train rated for the diagnostic pressure
proposals.why: The membrane vessels and second stage are the first limit: second-stage recovery is 0.1387 against 0.333 and feed pressure is capped at 75.84 bar (run baseline-cold-salty-1train). Existing RO-201 pressure ratings must not be raised; a new rated train, fed in parallel through a splitter and recombined through a mixer, is the physical route to the 95 bar diagnostic condition, and even then permeate salt was 0.529 g/L before the unmodelled second pass, so vendor performance must be confirmed.

changes.rating_source: vendor quote to confirm / standard size to be confirmed; membrane area and permeability are the logged model values from cold-salty-failing-baseline and are not stated in the 2004 study, so the rating and guaranteed recovery/TDS at 60 °F and 49,000 mg/L must come from the membrane vendor

field_checks.item: Guaranteed membrane performance at the cold, salty corner (water permeability, salt passage and required pressure at 60% recovery)
field_checks.where: Take a full ion analysis of Brownsville Ship Channel water at IN-101 during cold, high-salinity conditions and obtain a temperature-corrected vendor membrane projection / pilot result at 60 °F and 49,000 mg/L for RO-201
field_checks.changes: Decisive: the study does not print a full ion table or membrane area/flux (data sheet, Source water and Not in the study rows), and the model's recovery, pressure and salt results all rest on assumed membrane inputs. If the vendor projection reaches 60% at or below 75.84 bar with acceptable salt, the existing trains could pass and the new high-pressure equipment proposals would not be needed; if it needs about 95 bar, the no-go conclusion stands.

field_checks.item: Steam actually available to E-101 in cold weather, and the true pressure saving from heating
field_checks.where: Confirm steam header pressure, flow and temperature on line 5001 to E-101 with the co-located power plant, and get the heating benefit from the same vendor projection above
field_checks.changes: The study credits about 1% pressure reduction per °F heated (2004 PDF p.192), but the simulator's fixed-permeability model shows heating making recovery worse (runs heat-75F/90F/95F-per-train). If verified heating plus vendor membranes bring the required pressure within 75.84 bar, heating on the existing E-101 would become the cheapest fix and displace the new-equipment proposals.

field_checks.item: Nameplate confirmation of the pump motor, turbine coupling and vessel pressure rating
field_checks.where: Field nameplates on P-201 motor, T-201 Pelton turbine and RO-201 pressure vessels
field_checks.changes: Confirms the 2,900 HP motor and about 1,100 psig class used from 2004 PDF p.197; if installed vessels or pump are in fact rated materially above 95 bar, the fix could become an operating change instead of new equipment — do not assume this.

field_checks.item: Whether finished-water quality is met after the partial second pass
field_checks.where: Confirm the required finished-water salt and any boron limit with the owner and model or pilot RO-301 at the cold-corner first-pass permeate quality
field_checks.changes: The model checks first-pass permeate against 0.5 g/L and the second pass is note-only (check_coverage); the study picks no finished-water boron limit in the cited pages. If blending after RO-301 meets the real finished-water limit, only recovery/pressure need fixing; if not, second-pass capacity or membranes must be added to the fix.
